screens.title: Sending Transactions to Smart Contracts
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter we'll focus on write operations — the calls that actually change blockchain state. Unlike reads, these actions require a signed transaction, gas to execute, and time for the network to mine the result. You will learn the Web3. js pattern for initiating a transaction, how MetaMask prompts for signing, and the lifecycle events you can listen to so your dApp can give clear real-time feedback. We'll cover payable versus nonpayable functions and why converting Ether to Wei matters, and show code you can paste into a React hook to send a transaction and react to its transaction hash, receipt, or error. We'll also prepare you for common pitfalls: out-of-gas failures, network mismatches, and user cancellation inside MetaMask. By the end you'll be able to wire a form in your app to call a smart contract's setData function, display pending and confirmed states, and recover gracefully from errors. Think of this chapter as the practical bridge between a UI button and an irreversible change on-chain — you'll learn to make that bridge safe, transparent, and resilient.

screens.title: What you'll be able to do
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you'll initiate state-changing transactions from a React dApp, sign them securely through MetaMask, and present clear lifecycle feedback. First, you'll implement a send call that uses the current account and, for payable functions, a Wei value. Second, you'll wire listeners for transactionHash, receipt, and error so your interface reflects pending, confirmed, and failed states. Third, you'll recognize and handle common failures such as out-of-gas, network mismatches, and user rejections, and you'll know where to surface those messages in the UI. Finally, you'll apply safety practices: never request private keys from users, validate inputs client-side, and reason about idempotency for repeated calls. Each objective maps to a small milestone you can test locally: send a setData transaction, observe a transaction hash, handle a cancellation, and confirm contract state updated after receipt. These are practical, verifiable skills that keep your dApp resilient when it performs irreversible on-chain writes.

screens.title: Skills and validation milestones
screens.narratorSegment: This second objective slide describes how to validate your implementation and the micro-skills to practice. First, ensure the from address comes from your connected Web3 hook and is present before sending. If the function is payable, use web3. utils. toWei to convert Ether amounts into Wei; this conversion prevents precision errors and matches the blockchain's expected unit. Second, use event listeners to show progress: display the transaction hash immediately so a user can inspect it, then update the UI when the receipt arrives to reflect finality. Third, simulate common failure modes in a local or testnet environment: force an out-of-gas revert, switch networks to trigger chain mismatch, and cancel a MetaMask prompt to verify your rejection handling. Finally, measure idempotency for potentially repeated writes, and avoid asking users to re-submit the same operation without confirmation. These checkpoints give you concrete tests to confirm that your send function is robust and your UI communicates clearly and safely.

screens.title: What is a write operation?
screens.narratorSegment: A write operation is any smart contract function that modifies the blockchain state. Unlike view or pure functions that only read data and return immediately, write functions require a transaction to be formed, signed by the user's wallet, broadcast to the network, and mined into a block. This sequence consumes gas, which is paid in Ether. Concretely, a nonpayable function changes state but does not accept Ether; a payable function changes state and can receive Ether along with the call. A common misconception is that sending a transaction instantly updates your contract's state — it doesn't. You get a transaction hash right away when the transaction is broadcast, but the state change is only final once a mined receipt confirms success. For example, calling setData on a SimpleStorage contract will return immediately from your UI with a pending status and a transaction hash; only after the receipt arrives should you re-fetch the storedData value. Key takeaway: treat write calls as asynchronous, multi-step processes that require explicit UX states to avoid confusing users. What is a write operation? means write operations change on-chain state and require a signed, gas-paid transaction that must be mined to take effect.. In practical terms, why write calls require signing, gas, and mining. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Write operations change on-chain state and require a signed, gas-paid transaction that must be mined to take effect.

content.html:
Core Concept
Write operations
State-changing calls require a signed transaction, gas, and mining before state is final.
Quick points
  • Nonpayable: modifies state, accepts no Ether.
  • Payable: modifies state and accepts Ether via the value field.
  • .send() triggers MetaMask to prompt for signing and then broadcasts the transaction.
Example
Calling setData("new") on SimpleStorage will create a transaction. Show pending until receipt confirms and then re-fetch contract data.
Key Takeaway

Treat writes as asynchronous transactions: hash then receipt. Do not assume instant state change.

Analogy
Think of a write call as mailing a legal document. You get a shipment tracking number (transaction hash) immediately, but the legal effect occurs when the courier confirms delivery (receipt).
Common misconception
A transaction hash means success — incorrect. The hash indicates broadcast. Always wait for the receipt to confirm the state change.
Check your understanding
If you see a transaction hash but your UI still shows old data, what should you do? Wait for the receipt and then re-fetch on success; on error, show a clear message.

screens.title: Initiating a send() call and value conversion
screens.narratorSegment: To initiate a state-changing call in Web3. js you use the contract's methods and call. send with options. The minimal required option is the from address — the account that will sign and pay gas. If the function is payable, include a value field in Wei. Use web3. utils. toWei to convert Ether amounts into Wei; this avoids floating-point errors and matches the blockchain's expected base unit. A typical pattern looks like simpleStorageContract. methods. setData(newData). send({ from: currentAccount, value: web3. utils. toWei('0.1','ether') }). When this. send executes, MetaMask opens a confirmation showing recipient, value, and estimated gas. A common mistake is passing a human-readable Ether string directly into value without conversion, which will lead to wrong amounts or failures. Another detail: you can also specify gasLimit if you know a transaction will need more gas than the wallet estimates. In practice, place this call inside a try/catch and set UI flags for isSendingTransaction and transactionStatus so users see a sending indicator and final result. Now examine the code panel to the right and note how event listeners are chained to the same send call for lifecycle updates.

keyIdea.title: Practical pattern
keyIdea.text: Use contract.methods.f(...).send({ from, value: web3.utils.toWei(...) }) and always convert Ether to Wei before sending.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough
Initiating send()
Use the from option and convert Ether values to Wei. Handle errors with try/catch and update UI state flags.
Bulleted checklist
  • Ensure currentAccount is available.
  • For payable functions, call web3.utils.toWei(amount, 'ether').
  • Consider gasLimit only when automatic estimation fails.
Common mistake
Passing Ether as a plain string into value without toWei causes wrong unit and often failure.
Example code
const amountInWei = web3.utils.toWei('0.1', 'ether');
try {
  await simpleStorageContract.methods.setData(newData)
    .send({ from: currentAccount, value: amountInWei })
    .on('transactionHash', hash => console.log('hash', hash))
    .on('receipt', receipt => console.log('receipt', receipt))
    .on('error', err => console.error('error', err));
} catch (err) {
  console.error('send failed', err);
}
Example explained
We first convert 0.1 Ether to Wei, call setData and chain event listeners to react to lifecycle events. The try/catch catches rejections before or after the wallet prompt.

screens.title: Transaction lifecycle events
screens.narratorSegment: When you call. send() in Web3. js you can attach listeners to observe the transaction's lifecycle. The first event you'll commonly use is transactionHash, which fires as soon as the transaction is broadcast and gives you a hash. Use this to display a tracking link to a block explorer so users can inspect the pending transaction. Next comes the receipt event, triggered when the transaction is mined and included in a block; the receipt contains the block number, gas used, and a status flag indicating success or failure. Only after receipt should you change app state that depends on the new on-chain values. The error event captures any problem: a revert from the contract, a network issue, or a user cancellation in MetaMask. A typical UX pattern is to set transactionStatus to pending on transactionHash, to success on receipt, and to error on the error callback. A common misconception is treating the hash as final confirmation; it is not. Always rely on the receipt for finality and display clear messages for each stage to keep users informed. Transaction lifecycle events means transactionhash = broadcast, receipt = mined/final, error = failure or rejection. update ui at each stage.. In practical terms, transactionhash, receipt, and error explained. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Lifecycle
keyIdea.text: transactionHash = broadcast, receipt = mined/final, error = failure or rejection. Update UI at each stage.

content.html:
Process Flow
Transaction lifecycle
transactionHash: fired when broadcast; display hash and set pending state.
receipt: fired when mined; check status and gas used, then update contract-dependent UI.
error: fired on revert, network failure, or user rejection; show an actionable error and reset loading indicators.
Annotated sequence
1. Send
2. transactionHash
3. receipt / finality
Concrete example
After calling .send(), you receive a hash: display it with a link. When receipt arrives, confirm storedData updated and clear pending indicators. If error occurs, show the error message and allow retry.
Key Takeaway

Listen and respond to each lifecycle event; the receipt is the reliable confirmation of success.

screens.title: Payable vs nonpayable functions
screens.narratorSegment: Smart contract functions are labeled as payable when they accept Ether and nonpayable when they do not. This distinction matters at the call site because payable functions require you to include a value in the. send options when you want to transfer Ether along with the call. The common code mistake is forgetting web3. utils. toWei conversion or trying to send value to a nonpayable function, which will cause a revert. For example, calling deposit() on a payable function should include value: web3. utils. toWei('0.5','ether'), whereas a nonpayable setData should omit the value field. Another contrast: payable calls change both contract state and the contract balance, while nonpayable writes change only state. When designing UI, display an amount input only for payable actions and validate it before calling. send. Also present clear error messages if the user attempts to send Ether to a nonpayable function or provides an invalid amount. This comparison reduces user confusion and prevents avoidable failures. Payable vs nonpayable functions means payable accepts ether and needs value in wei; nonpayable does not. mismatching the two causes reverts.. In practical terms, when to include a value and how it affects .send() calls. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Payable vs Nonpayable
keyIdea.text: Payable accepts Ether and needs value in Wei; nonpayable does not. Mismatching the two causes reverts.

content.html:
Comparison
Payable vs Nonpayable
Payable: accepts Ether. Include value: web3.utils.toWei(...) when you want to send funds.
Nonpayable: does not accept Ether. Do not include a value or the call will revert.
UI guidance: show amount input only for payable actions and validate amount format.
Concrete scenario
If your contract has deposit() payable and setData(string) nonpayable, a deposit should include value in Wei; setData should only send a string. Sending value to setData will likely fail and waste gas in a failed transaction.
Misconception
Some developers assume value is in Ether. Always convert with toWei to avoid sending 0.1 wei instead of 0.1 Ether.
Key Takeaway

Match function mutability to the presence of value; always convert human values to Wei.

screens.title: Transaction Receipt and important fields
screens.narratorSegment: A TransactionReceipt is returned by the network once a transaction is mined. It contains several fields you should use in your dApp: the transaction hash, the blockNumber showing which block included the transaction, gasUsed telling you how much gas the transaction consumed, and a status flag that indicates success or failure. Checking gasUsed helps detect unexpectedly expensive calls. The status is especially important because a mined transaction can still fail on-chain if the EVM reverted; a receipt with status false means the state change did not occur even though it was included in a block. Use the receipt handler to re-fetch contract state when status is true and to surface a clear failure message when status is false. A common pitfall is trusting confirmations without inspecting the status. Another useful field is logs, which include event emissions you can read to update your UI more precisely. Always design your success path around a positive receipt. status and handle negative receipts as errors that may require manual investigation. Transaction Receipt and important fields means receipt shows blocknumber, gasused, status, and logs. use status to confirm success and logs for event-driven updates.. In practical terms, understanding block number, gas used, status, and why they matter. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Receipt fields
keyIdea.text: Receipt shows blockNumber, gasUsed, status, and logs. Use status to confirm success and logs for event-driven updates.

content.html:
Definition
TransactionReceipt
Key receipt fields let you confirm finality and inspect execution details.
blockNumber: which block included the transaction.
gasUsed: amount of gas consumed.
status: boolean indicating on-chain success or revert.
logs: event emissions you can parse to update app state.
Concrete example
After receipt arrives, check receipt.status. If true, call fetchContractData to refresh values. If false, show an error indicating a revert and suggest checking input values or gas settings.
Common pitfall

Treating a mined transaction as success without checking receipt.status can hide on-chain reverts.

Key Takeaway

Use receipt.status and logs to confirm success and update your dApp state reliably.

screens.title: Gas estimation and out-of-gas errors
screens.narratorSegment: Gas estimation is usually handled by MetaMask, but complex or dynamic contracts can produce incorrect estimates, leading to out-of-gas failures. If a transaction fails with an out-of-gas error, you may need to specify a higher gasLimit in the send options. However, guessing an arbitrarily large gasLimit is not ideal; instead, test on a local or testnet environment with representative inputs to measure typical gas usage, then set a sensible limit above that. Another approach is to call contract. methods. yourMethod(...). estimateGas({ from, value }) to get a programmatic estimate and add a safety margin before sending. A common misconception is to assume gasLimit prevents all failures; gasLimit only sets the maximum gas available — if contract logic reverts for another reason, the gasLimit won't prevent the revert. Always surface gas errors clearly to the user and suggest possible actions, such as retrying with a higher limit, checking input validity, or switching to a test environment for reproducing the issue. Gas estimation and out-of-gas errors means use estimategas when needed and increase gaslimit cautiously. test with realistic inputs to avoid out-of-gas failures.. In practical terms, when to rely on automatic gas estimation and when to set gaslimit manually. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Gas handling
keyIdea.text: Use estimateGas when needed and increase gasLimit cautiously. Test with realistic inputs to avoid out-of-gas failures.

content.html:
Common Mistake
Gas estimation
Use estimateGas to measure expected consumption and add a margin instead of guessing a huge gas limit.
Use: await contract.methods.foo().estimateGas({ from, value })
Then: .send({ from, gas: estimated + buffer })
Scenario
A complex loop in a contract might require more gas than MetaMask estimated. Use a local test run to measure gas for typical inputs and set a reasonable gasLimit based on that.
Pitfall

Increasing gasLimit without understanding contract logic can waste funds if transactions fail for reasons other than gas.

Key Takeaway

Estimate gas programmatically and add a margin; test on a testnet to choose safe limits.

screens.title: Handling user rejection and errors
screens.narratorSegment: Users sometimes cancel a MetaMask confirmation or a transaction reverts on-chain. Your code must handle both gracefully. When a user rejects the signature request, the. send Promise will reject and the error callback fires. Capture that error, set transactionStatus to a cancellation state, and show a clear message like 'Transaction cancelled by user.' For on-chain reverts, the receipt may show status false or the error event will include details about a revert. In those cases, present the revert reason if available or a friendly explanation and suggestions: check input values, increase gas if appropriate, or retry later. Avoid leaving the UI in a perpetual loading state. A helpful pattern is to centralize error handling in your sendSetDataTransaction function: set isSendingTransaction to true at start, set transactionStatus to pending on hash, to success on receipt, and to error with a useful message when catching an exception. Also log the raw error to console for debugging but present a sanitized message to users. This approach reduces confusion and encourages trust in your dApp. Handling user rejection and errors means catch user rejection and on-chain reverts, update transactional state flags, and show clear, actionable messages.. screens.title: Idempotency and safety of repeated writes
screens.narratorSegment: Idempotency means calling the same operation multiple times does not change the result beyond the initial call. For write operations this can greatly simplify UX around retries and accidental double-clicks. Consider a setData function: if it simply overwrites the stored value regardless, repeated calls may be harmless. But if a function triggers a state change that should happen only once, such as minting or transferring funds, repeated calls can cause duplicate effects. Where possible, design contract functions to be idempotent or add client-side checks that prevent accidental duplicates, like disabling the submit control while pending and storing recent transaction hashes to detect duplicates. In your hook, expose isSendingTransaction and transactionHash so the UI can prevent re-submission until the receipt arrives. A common misconception is assuming the network will deduplicate identical transactions; it will not. Planning for idempotency or explicit duplication checks reduces user errors and potential loss of funds. keyIdea.title: Hook pattern
keyIdea.text: Expose isSendingTransaction, transactionStatus, transactionHash, and sendSetDataTransaction from your hook for clean UI integration.

content.html:
Hands-on Activity
sendSetDataTransaction
This pattern sets flags, listens for events, and refreshes contract data on success.
Checklist
  • Guard for simpleStorageContract and currentAccount.
  • Set isSendingTransaction and transactionStatus before sending.
  • Chain on('transactionHash'), on('receipt'), on('error') and call fetchContractData on success.
Example hook snippet
const sendSetDataTransaction = useCallback(async (newData) => {
  if (!simpleStorageContract || !currentAccount) {
    setError('Contract or account not initialized for transaction.');
    return;
  }
  setIsSendingTransaction(true);
  setTransactionStatus('pending');
  setTransactionHash(null);
  setError(null);

  try {
    await simpleStorageContract.methods.setData(newData).send({ from: currentAccount })
      .on('transactionHash', hash => {
        setTransactionHash(hash);
      })
      .on('receipt', receipt => {
        setTransactionStatus('success');
        fetchContractData();
      })
      .on('error', (err) => {
        setTransactionStatus('error');
        setError(err.message || 'Transaction failed.');
      });
  } catch (err) {
    setTransactionStatus('error');
    setError(err.message || 'Transaction failed.');
  } finally {
    setIsSendingTransaction(false);
  }
}, [simpleStorageContract, currentAccount, fetchContractData]);

fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter we'll focus on write operations — the calls that actually change blockchain state. Unlike reads, these actions require a signed transaction, gas to execute, and time for the network to mine the result. You will learn the Web3. js pattern for initiating a transaction, how MetaMask prompts for signing, and the lifecycle events you can listen to so your dApp can give clear real-time feedback. We'll cover payable versus nonpayable functions and why converting Ether to Wei matters, and show code you can paste into a React hook to send a transaction and react to its transaction hash, receipt, or error. We'll also prepare you for common pitfalls: out-of-gas failures, network mismatches, and user cancellation inside MetaMask. By the end you'll be able to wire a form in your app to call a smart contract's setData function, display pending and confirmed states, and recover gracefully from errors. Think of this chapter as the practical bridge between a UI button and an irreversible change on-chain — you'll learn to make that bridge safe, transparent, and resilient.

By the end of this chapter you'll initiate state-changing transactions from a React dApp, sign them securely through MetaMask, and present clear lifecycle feedback. First, you'll implement a send call that uses the current account and, for payable functions, a Wei value. Second, you'll wire listeners for transactionHash, receipt, and error so your interface reflects pending, confirmed, and failed states. Third, you'll recognize and handle common failures such as out-of-gas, network mismatches, and user rejections, and you'll know where to surface those messages in the UI. Finally, you'll apply safety practices: never request private keys from users, validate inputs client-side, and reason about idempotency for repeated calls. Each objective maps to a small milestone you can test locally: send a setData transaction, observe a transaction hash, handle a cancellation, and confirm contract state updated after receipt. These are practical, verifiable skills that keep your dApp resilient when it performs irreversible on-chain writes.

This second objective slide describes how to validate your implementation and the micro-skills to practice. First, ensure the from address comes from your connected Web3 hook and is present before sending. If the function is payable, use web3. utils. toWei to convert Ether amounts into Wei; this conversion prevents precision errors and matches the blockchain's expected unit. Second, use event listeners to show progress: display the transaction hash immediately so a user can inspect it, then update the UI when the receipt arrives to reflect finality. Third, simulate common failure modes in a local or testnet environment: force an out-of-gas revert, switch networks to trigger chain mismatch, and cancel a MetaMask prompt to verify your rejection handling. Finally, measure idempotency for potentially repeated writes, and avoid asking users to re-submit the same operation without confirmation. These checkpoints give you concrete tests to confirm that your send function is robust and your UI communicates clearly and safely.

A write operation is any smart contract function that modifies the blockchain state. Unlike view or pure functions that only read data and return immediately, write functions require a transaction to be formed, signed by the user's wallet, broadcast to the network, and mined into a block. This sequence consumes gas, which is paid in Ether. Concretely, a nonpayable function changes state but does not accept Ether; a payable function changes state and can receive Ether along with the call. A common misconception is that sending a transaction instantly updates your contract's state — it doesn't. You get a transaction hash right away when the transaction is broadcast, but the state change is only final once a mined receipt confirms success. For example, calling setData on a SimpleStorage contract will return immediately from your UI with a pending status and a transaction hash; only after the receipt arrives should you re-fetch the storedData value. Key takeaway: treat write calls as asynchronous, multi-step processes that require explicit UX states to avoid confusing users. What is a write operation? means write operations change on-chain state and require a signed, gas-paid transaction that must be mined to take effect.. In practical terms, why write calls require signing, gas, and mining. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

To initiate a state-changing call in Web3. js you use the contract's methods and call. send with options. The minimal required option is the from address — the account that will sign and pay gas. If the function is payable, include a value field in Wei. Use web3. utils. toWei to convert Ether amounts into Wei; this avoids floating-point errors and matches the blockchain's expected base unit. A typical pattern looks like simpleStorageContract. methods. setData(newData). send({ from: currentAccount, value: web3. utils. toWei('0.1','ether') }). When this. send executes, MetaMask opens a confirmation showing recipient, value, and estimated gas. A common mistake is passing a human-readable Ether string directly into value without conversion, which will lead to wrong amounts or failures. Another detail: you can also specify gasLimit if you know a transaction will need more gas than the wallet estimates. In practice, place this call inside a try/catch and set UI flags for isSendingTransaction and transactionStatus so users see a sending indicator and final result. Now examine the code panel to the right and note how event listeners are chained to the same send call for lifecycle updates.

When you call. send() in Web3. js you can attach listeners to observe the transaction's lifecycle. The first event you'll commonly use is transactionHash, which fires as soon as the transaction is broadcast and gives you a hash. Use this to display a tracking link to a block explorer so users can inspect the pending transaction. Next comes the receipt event, triggered when the transaction is mined and included in a block; the receipt contains the block number, gas used, and a status flag indicating success or failure. Only after receipt should you change app state that depends on the new on-chain values. The error event captures any problem: a revert from the contract, a network issue, or a user cancellation in MetaMask. A typical UX pattern is to set transactionStatus to pending on transactionHash, to success on receipt, and to error on the error callback. A common misconception is treating the hash as final confirmation; it is not. Always rely on the receipt for finality and display clear messages for each stage to keep users informed. Transaction lifecycle events means transactionhash = broadcast, receipt = mined/final, error = failure or rejection. update ui at each stage.. In practical terms, transactionhash, receipt, and error explained. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Smart contract functions are labeled as payable when they accept Ether and nonpayable when they do not. This distinction matters at the call site because payable functions require you to include a value in the. send options when you want to transfer Ether along with the call. The common code mistake is forgetting web3. utils. toWei conversion or trying to send value to a nonpayable function, which will cause a revert. Idempotency means calling the same operation multiple times does not change the result beyond the initial call.
